---
title: "Mathematical Foundations"
subtitle: "The First-Principles Equations Behind Every MLSys·im Solver"
---

MLSys·im avoids "black box" heuristics. Every output traces back to one of the equations below.
Read this page before the code to understand *what* the solvers compute and *why*.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import math
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models, Infrastructure, Systems, Literature, Q_
from mlsysim.solvers import DistributedModel, ContinuousBatchingModel
from mlsysim.systems.types import Fleet
from mlsysim.physics import (
    calc_ring_allreduce_time,
    calc_pipeline_bubble,
    calc_transformer_training_flops,
    calc_young_daly_interval,
    calc_failure_probability,
)
from mlsysim.engine.calibration import TRAINING_OPTIMIZER_BYTES_ADAM

_a100 = Hardware.Cloud.A100
_h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
_l8 = Models.Language.Llama3_8B
_l70 = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
_gpt3 = Models.Language.GPT3

_a100_peak = _a100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
_a100_bw = _a100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
_a100_ridge = (_a100.compute.peak_flops / _a100.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude
_a100_tdp = _a100.tdp.to("W").magnitude

_h100_peak = _h100.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
_h100_bw = _h100.memory.bandwidth.to("TB/s").magnitude
_h100_cap_gib = _h100.memory.capacity.to("GiB").magnitude
_h100_ridge = (_h100.compute.peak_flops / _h100.memory.bandwidth).to("flop/byte").magnitude

_hdr = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_HDR
_dgx_a100 = Systems.Nodes.DGX_A100
_gpt3_eff = {}
for _n in [64, 256, 1024, 8192]:
    _fl = Fleet(name=f"A100-{_n}", node=_dgx_a100, count=_n // 8, fabric=_hdr)
    _dp = _n // 64
    _gpt3_eff[_n] = DistributedModel().solve(
        model=_gpt3, fleet=_fl, batch_size=1536, tp_size=8, pp_size=8,
        microbatch_count=1536 // _dp, seq_len=2048
    ).scaling_efficiency * 100

_ndr_bw_gbs = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude
_eth100_bw_gbs = Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_100G.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude
_ar_140_bw_s = (2 * 1023 / 1024) * (140.0 / _ndr_bw_gbs)
_ar_140_lat_ms = (2 * 1023 * 2.0) / 1000.0
_ar_140_tot_s = calc_ring_allreduce_time(Q_("140 GB"), 1024, Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth, Q_("2 us")).to("s").magnitude

_bub_4_16_1 = calc_pipeline_bubble(4, 16, v_stages=1) * 100
_bub_4_16_2 = calc_pipeline_bubble(4, 16, v_stages=2) * 100
_bub_8_32_1 = calc_pipeline_bubble(8, 32, v_stages=1) * 100
_bub_16_16_1 = calc_pipeline_bubble(16, 16, v_stages=1) * 100

_gpt3_params_b = _gpt3.parameters.to("Bparam").magnitude
_gpt3_tokens_b = _gpt3.training_tokens.to("Btoken").magnitude
_gpt3_flops = calc_transformer_training_flops(_gpt3.parameters, _gpt3.training_tokens).to("flop").magnitude
_gpt3_train_s = _gpt3_flops / (1024 * _a100.compute.peak_flops.to("flop/s").magnitude * 0.5)
_gpt3_train_days = _gpt3_train_s / 86400
_adam_opt_bytes = int(TRAINING_OPTIMIZER_BYTES_ADAM)

_l70_params_b = _l70.parameters.to("Bparam").magnitude
_l70_wt_gb = _l70.size_in_bytes("fp16").to("GB").magnitude
_l70_cmp_ms = (_l70.inference_flops / _h100.compute.peak_flops).to("ms").magnitude
_l70_mem_ms = (_l70.size_in_bytes("fp16") / _h100.memory.bandwidth).to("ms").magnitude
_l70_tok_s = 1000.0 / _l70_mem_ms

_l70_layers = _l70.layers
_l70_heads = _l70.heads
_l70_kv_heads = _l70.kv_heads
_l70_gqa_ratio = _l70_heads // _l70_kv_heads
_l70_d_head = _l70.hidden_dim // _l70_heads
_l70_kv_tok_kb = _l70.get_kv_cache_size(1, 1, "fp16").to("KB").magnitude
_l70_kv_b16_gb = _l70.get_kv_cache_size(4096, 16, "fp16").to("GB").magnitude
_l70_kv_b32_gb = _l70.get_kv_cache_size(4096, 32, "fp16").to("GB").magnitude
_l70_wt_int4_gb = _l70.size_in_bytes("int4").to("GB").magnitude
_l70_tot_b32_gb = _l70_wt_int4_gb + _l70_kv_b32_gb

_l8_kv_tok_b = int(_l8.get_kv_cache_size(1, 1, "fp16").to("byte").magnitude)
_h100_kv_budget_tok = int(((_h100.memory.capacity - _l8.size_in_bytes("fp16")) / Q_(_l8_kv_tok_b, "byte")).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
_cb_8k_16 = ContinuousBatchingModel().solve(model=_l8, hardware=_h100, max_seq_len=8192, mean_request_tokens=2048, max_batch_size=1000, page_size=16, precision="fp16")
_cb_8k_2048 = ContinuousBatchingModel().solve(model=_l8, hardware=_h100, max_seq_len=8192, mean_request_tokens=2048, max_batch_size=1000, page_size=2048, precision="fp16")

_grids = Infrastructure.Grids
_ci_quebec = _grids.Quebec.carbon_intensity_g_kwh
_ci_us = _grids.US_Avg.carbon_intensity_g_kwh
_ci_poland = _grids.Poland.carbon_intensity_g_kwh
_ci_spread = _ci_poland / _ci_quebec
_it_kwh = 64 * (_a100_tdp / 1000.0) * 336
_tot_kwh = _it_kwh * 1.2
_co2_quebec = _tot_kwh * _ci_quebec / 1000.0
_co2_us = _tot_kwh * _ci_us / 1000.0
_co2_poland = _tot_kwh * _ci_poland / 1000.0

_dgx_cost_k = Infrastructure.Pricing.Capital.DgxH100NodeUsd.rate.magnitude / 1000.0
_amort_yr = int(Infrastructure.Pricing.Capital.AcceleratorServiceLifeYears.rate)
_cloud_gpu_hr = Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.GpuTrainingPerHour.rate.magnitude
_h100_a100_flops_ratio = _h100_peak / _a100_peak

_gpu_mttf_hr = Systems.Reliability.Gpu.mttf_hours
_mtbf_1k_hr = _gpu_mttf_hr / 1000
_mtbf_10k_hr = _gpu_mttf_hr / 10000
_mtbf_16k_hr = _gpu_mttf_hr / 16000
_llama3_16k_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Meta_Llama3_16K_H100.total_accelerators
_llama3_failures = int(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_UnexpectedInterruptions)
_llama3_days = int(Literature.TrainingRuns.Llama3_405B_SnapshotDays)
_tau_opt_min = calc_young_daly_interval(Q_("2 min"), Q_("180 min")).to("min").magnitude
_prob_30d = calc_failure_probability(Q_("5 hour"), Q_("720 hour"))
```

## 1. The Roofline Model (Single-Node Performance) {#sec-roofline}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.SingleNodeModel`](api/solvers.SingleNodeModel.qmd).*
**Slide Deck:** [Hardware Acceleration (Vol I, Ch 11)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol1_11_hw_acceleration.pdf){target="_blank"}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Intuition:** Hardware has two speed limits: how fast it can compute (FLOP/s) and how fast it can feed data to the compute units (bytes/s). Actual throughput is set by whichever limit is reached first. This is why we take the *maximum* of two terms, not their sum.
:::

### 1.1 Latency Equation

$$
T = \max \left( \underbrace{\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta}}_{\text{compute time}},\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{Bytes}}{\text{Memory\_BW}}}_{\text{memory time}} \right) + \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical Range |
|:-------|:--------|:--------------|
| $\eta$ | Achieved compute efficiency | 0.25–0.55 (training); ~0.35 (inference). See [Accuracy & Validation](accuracy.qmd). |
| Dispatch\_Tax | Kernel-launch overhead (CUDA, driver) | 0.01–0.1 ms |

### 1.2 Arithmetic Intensity and the Ridge Point

The key diagnostic ratio is **arithmetic intensity**:

$$
I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes Transferred}}
$$

The **ridge point** is the hardware's crossover intensity:

$$
I^* = \frac{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s}}{\text{Memory\_BW}}
$$

| If... | Regime | Action |
|:------|:-------|:-------|
| $I > I^*$ | **Compute-bound** | Faster math units, lower precision, or fewer FLOPs |
| $I < I^*$ | **Memory-bound** | Larger batch size, operator fusion, or higher memory bandwidth |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: Dense Layer on H100

A dense layer with 2048→512, FP16, batch=1:

- **FLOPs:** $2 \times 2048 \times 512 = 2.1\text{M}$
- **Bytes:** $2048 \times 512 \times 2 = 2.1\text{MB}$
- **Arithmetic Intensity:** $2.1\text{M} / 2.1\text{MB} = 1$ FLOP/byte
- **H100 Ridge Point:** $`{python} f"{_h100_peak:.0f}"`\text{ TF} / `{python} f"{_h100_bw:.2f}"`\text{ TB/s} \approx `{python} f"{_h100_ridge:.0f}"`$ FLOP/byte (vs. $`{python} f"{_a100_peak:.0f}"`\text{ TF} / `{python} f"{_a100_bw:.2f}"`\text{ TB/s} \approx `{python} f"{_a100_ridge:.0f}"`$ FLOP/byte on A100)

At $I = 1 \ll `{python} f"{_h100_ridge:.0f}"` = I^*$, this workload is **deeply memory-bound**. The H100 achieves <1% of peak compute. Increasing to batch=64 raises $I$ to ~64, recovering significant throughput.

Source: Slide deck worked example, Vol I Ch 11.
:::

## 2. Distributed Training (3D/4D Parallelism) {#sec-distributed}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.DistributedModel`](api/solvers.DistributedModel.qmd).*
**Slide Decks:** [Distributed Training (Vol II, Ch 6)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_06_distributed_training.pdf){target="_blank"} | [Collective Communication (Vol II, Ch 5)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_05_collective_communication.pdf){target="_blank"}

Real distributed training involves complex interactions between computation, communication, and scheduling. Empirical profiling requires access to expensive multi-GPU clusters and takes hours per configuration. MLSys·im decomposes the problem into independent overheads, each governed by a closed-form equation, so thousands of parallelism configurations can be evaluated in seconds.

### 2.1 Parallelism Decomposition

MLSys·im supports 4D parallelism. Given a cluster of $N$ total GPUs:

$$
\text{DP} = \frac{N}{\text{TP} \times \text{PP} \times \text{EP}}
$$

| Dimension | What It Splits | Communication Pattern |
|:----------|:---------------|:---------------------|
| **Data Parallelism (DP)** | Batch across replicas | AllReduce (gradients) |
| **Tensor Parallelism (TP)** | Individual layers across GPUs | Point-to-point (intra-node NVLink) |
| **Pipeline Parallelism (PP)** | Layer groups across stages | Forward/backward activations |
| **Expert Parallelism (EP)** | MoE experts across GPUs | All-to-All (token routing) |

### 2.2 Scaling Efficiency

The solver computes an overall **scaling efficiency**, the fraction of ideal linear speedup actually achieved:

$$
\eta_{\text{scale}} = \frac{T_{\text{compute}}}{T_{\text{compute}} + T_{\text{dp}} + T_{\text{tp}} + T_{\text{ep}} + T_{\text{bubble}}}
$$

An efficiency of 80% on 256 GPUs delivers the throughput of ~`{python} f"{int(round(0.80 * 256))}"` GPUs; the rest is lost to communication and pipeline bubbles. For the GPT-3 `{python} f"{_gpt3_params_b:.0f}B"` reference job (eight-way tensor and eight-way pipeline parallelism on HDR InfiniBand, fixed GPT-3 batch of 1,536 sequences), the solver predicts about `{python} f"{_gpt3_eff[64]:.0f}%"` at 64 GPUs, `{python} f"{_gpt3_eff[256]:.0f}%"` at 256, `{python} f"{_gpt3_eff[1024]:.0f}%"` at 1,024, and `{python} f"{_gpt3_eff[8192]:.0f}%"` at 8,192, where the pipeline bubble dominates. Production systems with larger batches and interleaved pipelines retain more. MegaScale's 175B MFU falls only from 59.1% to 55.2% between 3,072 and 12,288 GPUs [@jiang2024megascale].

### 2.3 Ring All-Reduce (Data Parallelism) {#sec-allreduce}

**Slide Deck:** [Collective Communication (Vol II, Ch 5)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_05_collective_communication.pdf){target="_blank"}

After each training step, every GPU must synchronize gradients. The standard algorithm is **ring all-reduce**, which arranges $N$ GPUs in a logical ring and passes gradient chunks in two phases (scatter-reduce, then all-gather).

Using the $\alpha$-$\beta$ communication model ($\alpha$ = per-message latency, $\beta$ = bandwidth):

$$
T_{\text{ring}} = 2(N-1) \cdot \alpha \;+\; \frac{2(N-1)}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------|:--------|
| $M$ | Total gradient size in bytes |
| $N$ | Number of GPUs in the ring |
| $\alpha$ | Per-message startup latency |
| $\beta$ | Per-link bandwidth (bytes/s) |

**Why ring all-reduce scales well:** The bandwidth term $\frac{2(N-1)}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}$ approaches $\frac{2M}{\beta}$ as $N$ grows, so it is asymptotically **constant** in the number of GPUs. Total data transferred per GPU is always ~$2M$, regardless of cluster size. The latency term $2(N-1) \cdot \alpha$ grows linearly, but is negligible for large messages.

MLSys·im also implements **tree all-reduce** (latency-optimal for small messages):

$$
T_{\text{tree}} = 2 \log_2(N) \cdot \alpha \;+\; 2 \log_2(N) \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
$$

The crossover point between ring and tree is approximately $M_{\text{cross}} \approx N \cdot \alpha \cdot \beta$. Below this size, tree wins (latency dominates); above it, ring wins (bandwidth dominates).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: 140 GB Gradient Sync

A 70B-parameter model in FP16 produces a 140 GB gradient. On a 1,024-GPU cluster with InfiniBand NDR ($\beta = `{python} f"{_ndr_bw_gbs:.0f}"`$ GB/s, $\alpha = 2\;\mu$s):

- **Bandwidth term:** $\frac{2 \times 1023}{1024} \times \frac{140}{`{python} f"{_ndr_bw_gbs:.0f}"`} \approx `{python} f"{_ar_140_bw_s:.1f}"`$ s
- **Latency term:** $2 \times 1023 \times 2\;\mu\text{s} \approx `{python} f"{_ar_140_lat_ms:.0f}"`$ ms (negligible)
- **Total:** ~`{python} f"{_ar_140_tot_s:.1f}"` s, bandwidth-dominated as expected for large messages.

Upgrading from 100 Gb Ethernet (~`{python} f"{_eth100_bw_gbs:.1f}"` GB/s) to NDR (~`{python} f"{_ndr_bw_gbs:.0f}"` GB/s) recovers 10–30% scaling efficiency.
:::

### 2.4 Pipeline Parallelism Bubble {#sec-pipeline}

**Slide Deck:** [Distributed Training (Vol II, Ch 6)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_06_distributed_training.pdf){target="_blank"}

**Pipeline parallelism** splits a model's layers across $P$ stages. At the start of each batch, downstream stages sit idle while upstream stages produce output. This idle time is the **pipeline bubble**.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Intuition:** The speed of light is fixed, but the software schedule *can* change. Assigning multiple **virtual stages** ($V$) to each GPU interleaves execution: while a GPU waits for one virtual stage's next microbatch, it computes a different virtual stage's microbatch, hiding latency behind useful work.
:::

With $P$ pipeline stages, $M$ microbatches, and $V$ virtual stages per GPU:

$$
\text{Bubble Fraction} = \frac{P - 1}{V \times M + P - 1}
$$

| Configuration | Bubble Fraction |
|:-------------|:----------------|
| $P=4, M=16, V=1$ | $3/19 = `{python} f"{_bub_4_16_1:.1f}"`\%$ |
| $P=4, M=16, V=2$ | $3/35 = `{python} f"{_bub_4_16_2:.1f}"`\%$ |
| $P=8, M=32, V=1$ | $7/39 = `{python} f"{_bub_8_32_1:.1f}"`\%$ |
| $P=16, M=16, V=1$ | $15/31 = `{python} f"{_bub_16_16_1:.1f}"`\%$ (unacceptable) |

Keeping the bubble below 5% with standard 1F1B ($V=1$) requires $M \geq 19 \times (P - 1)$ microbatches. Interleaved schedules ($V \geq 2$) cut this requirement proportionally.

### 2.5 Expert Parallelism (Mixture of Experts) {#sec-moe}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Intuition:** Dense Transformers obey a strict "Iron Law": doubling parameters doubles both memory *and* compute. Mixture of Experts (MoE) breaks this law by routing tokens to specific expert subnetworks. The **memory bound** is set by the *total* parameters, but the **compute bound** is set by the much smaller *active* parameters. The physical tradeoff is a network bandwidth tax (All-to-All communication) to route tokens across the cluster.
:::

When $\text{EP} > 1$, the solver adds an **All-to-All** communication penalty for token routing:

$$
T_{\text{all-to-all}} = (N-1) \cdot \alpha \;+\; \frac{N-1}{N} \cdot \frac{M}{\beta}
$$

where $N$ is the EP degree. Compared to AllReduce, All-to-All creates $O(N^2)$ point-to-point connections, making it **latency-sensitive**. A 4 KB token routing message is latency-bound, while a 140 GB gradient sync is bandwidth-bound.

MoE routing is rarely perfectly balanced. MLSys·im exposes a single routing-imbalance factor $\gamma \ge 1$:

$$
E_{\text{active,eff}} = \min(E_{\text{total}}, \gamma \cdot E_{\text{top-k}})
$$

$$
P_{\text{active,eff}} = P_{\text{active}} \cdot \frac{E_{\text{active,eff}}}{E_{\text{top-k}}}
$$

`MoERoutingModel` reports the effective active experts, effective active parameters, routed bytes, and optional expert-parallel all-to-all latency. This is a first-order hot-expert proxy, not a router simulation; it is intended to capture the load-balancing concern surfaced by sparsely-gated MoE, GShard, and Switch-style systems [@shazeer2017outrageously; @lepikhin2020gshard; @fedus2022switch].

## 3. Training Scaling Laws {#sec-scaling}

*Used by [`mlsysim.physics.calc_transformer_training_flops`]({{< var github_repo >}}/blob/dev/mlsysim/mlsysim/physics/).*
**Slide Deck:** [Training (Vol I, Ch 8)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol1_08_training.pdf){target="_blank"}

The **6PD rule** estimates total training FLOPs for a Transformer:

$$
C \approx 6 \times P \times D
$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------|:--------|
| $C$ | Total training FLOPs |
| $P$ | Number of model parameters |
| $D$ | Number of training tokens |

The factor of 6 is 2 FLOPs per parameter per token (forward pass multiply-accumulate) × 3 passes (forward + backward for weights + backward for activations). Combined with the roofline model ([Section 1](#sec-roofline)), this gives training time:

$$
T_{\text{train}} = \frac{6PD}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta}
$$

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: GPT-3 Training Time

GPT-3 `{python} f"{_gpt3_params_b:.0f}B"` trained on `{python} f"{_gpt3_tokens_b:.0f}B"` tokens:

- **Total FLOPs:** $6 \times `{python} f"{_gpt3_params_b:.0f}"` \times 10^9 \times `{python} f"{_gpt3_tokens_b:.0f}"` \times 10^9 = `{python} f"{_gpt3_flops / 1e23:.2f}"` \times 10^{23}$
- **On 1,024 A100s** ($`{python} f"{_a100_peak:.0f}"`\text{ TF each} \times 0.5$ MFU): $`{python} f"{_gpt3_flops / 1e23:.2f}"` \times 10^{23} / (1024 \times `{python} f"{_a100_peak:.0f}"` \times 10^{12} \times 0.5) \approx `{python} f"{_gpt3_train_s / 1e6:.2f}"` \times 10^6\text{ s} \approx `{python} f"{_gpt3_train_days:.0f}"`\text{ days}$

Narayanan et al. estimate about 34 days for this configuration [@narayanan2021]. The gap from `{python} f"{_gpt3_train_days:.0f}"` days is not a scaling loss. Their estimate counts 8 FLOPs per parameter per token, because activation recomputation repeats the forward pass, and it uses a measured 140 TFLOP/s per GPU (about 45% of peak), which already includes communication and pipeline losses.
:::

### 3.1 Training Memory Accounting {#sec-training-memory}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.TrainingMemoryModel`](api/solvers.TrainingMemoryModel.qmd).*

Inference memory is mostly weights plus KV cache. Training memory adds gradients, optimizer state, saved activations, and communication buffers:

$$
M_{\text{train}} =
M_{\text{weights}} + M_{\text{grad}} + M_{\text{opt}} +
M_{\text{act}} + M_{\text{comm}}
$$

For mixed-precision Adam training, the default per-parameter state is:

| Component | Default bytes / parameter | ZeRO sharding |
|:----------|--------------------------:|:--------------|
| Weights | 2 | Stage 3 |
| Gradients | 2 | Stage 2+ |
| Adam optimizer state | `{python} f"{_adam_opt_bytes}"` | Stage 1+ |

Tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism first shard the model states across model-parallel ranks. ZeRO then shards data-parallel states [@rajbhandari2020]. Activation memory scales with local microbatch size, sequence length, hidden dimension, and the chosen activation-checkpointing strategy [@korthikanti2023].

## 4. LLM Serving Lifecycle {#sec-serving}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.ServingModel`](api/solvers.ServingModel.qmd).*
**Slide Decks:** [Model Serving (Vol I, Ch 13)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol1_13_model_serving.pdf){target="_blank"} | [Inference at Scale (Vol II, Ch 10)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_10_inference.pdf){target="_blank"}

LLM autoregressive inference has two physically distinct phases. Capacity planning depends on knowing which phase dominates.

### 4.1 Pre-fill Phase (Compute-Bound)

The initial forward pass processes all prompt tokens in parallel:

$$
\text{TTFT} = \frac{2 \times P \times S \times B}{\text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \eta} + \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------|:--------|
| $P$ | Number of model parameters |
| $S$ | Input sequence length |
| $B$ | Batch size |

The factor of 2 counts both the multiply and the add in each multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation.

### 4.2 Decoding Phase (Memory-Bound) {#sec-decode}

Each decode step loads the entire model weight matrix plus the accumulated KV-cache:

$$
\text{ITL} = \frac{\text{Model\_Bytes} + \text{KV\_Cache\_Bytes}}{\text{Memory\_BW}}
$$

This phase is almost always **memory-bound** because generating one token requires loading the full weight matrix but performs far fewer FLOPs (a single matrix-vector product per layer). On an H100 at batch=1, compute takes ~3% of the time; memory loading takes ~97%.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: Llama-3 70B Decode on H100

Single-token decode, batch=1 (`{python} f"{_l70_params_b:.1f}B"` parameters, `{python} f"{_l70_wt_gb:.1f} GB"` in FP16):

- **Compute:** $2 \times `{python} f"{_l70_params_b:.1f}"`\text{B} / `{python} f"{_h100_peak:.0f}"`\text{ TF} = `{python} f"{_l70_cmp_ms:.2f}"`\text{ ms}$ (0.3% of memory time)
- **Memory:** $`{python} f"{_l70_wt_gb:.1f}"`\text{ GB} / `{python} f"{_h100_bw:.2f}"`\text{ TB/s} = `{python} f"{_l70_mem_ms:.1f}"`\text{ ms}$
- **Total:** ~`{python} f"{_l70_mem_ms:.0f}"` ms/token → ~`{python} f"{_l70_tok_s:.0f}"` tokens/s

The decode phase is so memory-bound that a hypothetical 2× compute upgrade yields zero speedup. Only higher memory bandwidth (or batching) helps.

Source: Compute Infrastructure slides (Vol II, Ch 2).
:::

### 4.3 KV-Cache Size {#sec-kvcache}

$$
\text{KV\_Bytes} = 2 \times L \times H_{\text{kv}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times S \times B \times b_{\text{elem}}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------|:--------|
| $L$ | Number of Transformer layers |
| $H_{\text{kv}}$ | Number of KV attention heads (equals $H$ for MHA; smaller for GQA/MQA) |
| $d_{\text{head}}$ | Dimension per head |
| $S$ | Sequence length |
| $B$ | Batch size |
| $b_{\text{elem}}$ | Bytes per element (2 for FP16/BF16) |

The factor of 2 accounts for both the K and V tensors. With **Grouped-Query Attention** (GQA), $H_{\text{kv}} < H$, which reduces cache size. Llama-3 70B uses `{python} f"{_l70_kv_heads}"` KV heads vs. `{python} f"{_l70_heads}"` query heads, an `{python} f"{_l70_gqa_ratio}"`× reduction.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: KV-Cache Capacity Planning

Llama-3 70B: `{python} f"{_l70_layers}"` layers, `{python} f"{_l70_kv_heads}"` KV heads (GQA), $d_{\text{head}} = `{python} f"{_l70_d_head}"`$, FP16:

- **Per-token:** $2 \times `{python} f"{_l70_layers}"` \times `{python} f"{_l70_kv_heads}"` \times `{python} f"{_l70_d_head}"` \times 2 = `{python} f"{_l70_kv_tok_kb:.1f}"`\text{ KB}$
- **Batch=16, seq=4096:** $`{python} f"{_l70_kv_tok_kb:.1f}"`\text{K} \times 16 \times 4096 = `{python} f"{_l70_kv_b16_gb:.1f}"`\text{ GB}$
- **Batch=32, seq=4096:** $`{python} f"{_l70_kv_tok_kb:.1f}"`\text{K} \times 32 \times 4096 = `{python} f"{_l70_kv_b32_gb:.1f}"`\text{ GB}$

Weights (`{python} f"{_l70_wt_int4_gb:.1f}"` GB at INT4) + KV-cache (`{python} f"{_l70_kv_b32_gb:.1f}"` GB at FP16) = `{python} f"{_l70_tot_b32_gb:.1f}"` GB, which barely fits on an `{python} f"{_h100_cap_gib:.0f}"` GiB H100. At batch=64 or longer contexts, the model must be sharded across multiple GPUs.

Source: Inference at Scale slides (Vol II, Ch 10).
:::

### 4.4 Chunked Prefill and Decode Interference {#sec-chunked-prefill}

Production serving systems often mix new prefill work with ongoing decode iterations. Long prefills can stall decode unless the scheduler bounds the amount of prefill work admitted per iteration. MLSys·im models this with an optional prefill chunk size. Let $S_{\text{new}} = S - S_{\text{cache}}$, with $0 \le S_{\text{cache}} < S$ and $S_{\text{chunk}} > 0$:

$$
C = \left\lceil \frac{S_{\text{new}}}{S_{\text{chunk}}} \right\rceil
$$

$$
\text{TTFT}_{\text{chunked}} =
\text{TTFT}_{\text{compute}} + C \times \text{Dispatch\_Tax}
$$

$$
\text{Decode\_Stall}_{\max} \approx
\max_i\left(T_{\text{chunk},i}\right)
$$

Here $T_{\text{chunk},i}$ is the compute time for chunk $i$ plus one dispatch tax.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------|:--------|
| $C$ | Number of prefill chunks |
| $S_{\text{new}}$ | Prompt tokens that still require prefill computation |
| $S_{\text{cache}}$ | Prompt tokens already covered by prefix caching |
| $S_{\text{chunk}}$ | Maximum prefill tokens admitted per scheduler iteration |

This estimates a coarse scheduling proxy used by chunked-prefill systems: smaller chunks do not reduce total prefill compute, but they reduce the largest decode stall caused by a co-scheduled prefill. MLSys·im does not implement Sarathi-Serve's full scheduler. Disaggregated systems such as Splitwise and DistServe mitigate prefill/decode interference by assigning the phases to separate resources, trading scheduler interference for KV-cache transfer and resource-partitioning costs [@agrawal2025; @patel2024; @zhong2024distserve].

### 4.5 KV Allocation and Batch Capacity {#sec-batching}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.ContinuousBatchingModel`](api/solvers.ContinuousBatchingModel.qmd).*

Decode is memory-bound, so the number of requests sharing a step is the throughput lever, and the KV-cache allocator decides how many fit. Let $M_{\text{KV}}$ be the HBM left after the weights and $k$ the KV bytes per token ([KV-Cache Size](#sec-kvcache)). A static allocator reserves the maximum sequence length $S_{\max}$ for every request. A paged allocator divides the budget into blocks of $p$ tokens and hands a request of $S$ tokens $\lceil S/p \rceil$ of them on demand:

$$
N_{\text{static}} = \left\lfloor \frac{M_{\text{KV}}}{k\,S_{\max}} \right\rfloor
\qquad
N_{\text{paged}} = \left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor M_{\text{KV}} / (k\,p) \rfloor}{\mathbb{E}\left[\lceil S/p \rceil\right]} \right\rfloor
$$

The scheduler's maximum batch size caps both. Request lengths are $S = \min(X, S_{\max})$ with $X$ exponential, scaled so that $\mathbb{E}[S] = \bar{S}$: most requests are short, and the rare long one is cut off at the context window. Summing tail probabilities gives the expected block count in closed form

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\lceil S/p \rceil\right] = \sum_{j=0}^{K-1} P(S > jp) = \frac{1 - r^{K}}{1 - r},
\qquad r = e^{-p/\mu},\quad K = \lceil S_{\max}/p \rceil
$$

The unused share of each allocation (internal fragmentation) is $1 - \bar{S}/S_{\max}$ for static reservation and $1 - \bar{S}/\left(p\,\mathbb{E}[\lceil S/p \rceil]\right)$ for paging. The paged tail averages about $p/2$ tokens per request, so page size matters even when $S_{\max}$ divides evenly by $p$. Memory-bound decode streams only the tokens requests have filled, so for either allocator

$$
t_{\text{step}} = \frac{|W| + N\,\bar{S}\,k}{\text{Memory\_BW}},
\qquad R_{\text{tok}} = \frac{N}{t_{\text{step}}}
$$

and `speedup_vs_static` is $R_{\text{tok}}$ at $N_{\text{paged}}$ divided by $R_{\text{tok}}$ at $N_{\text{static}}$.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------|:--------|
| $M_{\text{KV}}$ | HBM capacity left for the KV cache after the weights |
| $k$ | KV bytes per token |
| $S_{\max}$ | Longest context a request may reach (`max_seq_len`) |
| $\bar{S}$ | Mean tokens a request fills (`mean_request_tokens`; defaults to $S_{\max}$) |
| $p$ | Block (page) size in tokens (`page_size`) |
| $\mu$ | Exponential scale chosen so that $\mathbb{E}[\min(X, S_{\max})] = \bar{S}$ |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: Llama-3 8B on H100 with an 8K Context

FP16 KV costs $k = `{python} f"{_l8_kv_tok_b:,}"`$ bytes per token, so the H100's KV budget holds about `{python} f"{_h100_kv_budget_tok:,}"` tokens. With $S_{\max} = 8192$ and $\bar{S} = 2048$:

- **Static reservation:** $\lfloor `{python} f"{_h100_kv_budget_tok:,}"` / 8192 \rfloor = `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.static_max_active_requests}"`$ requests, with `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.static_internal_fragmentation * 100:.0f}%"` of every reservation unused
- **Paged, $p = 16$:** about 128.5 blocks per request, so `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.max_active_requests}"` requests with `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.paged_internal_fragmentation * 100:.1f}%"` unused
- **Paged, $p = 2048$:** `{python} f"{_cb_8k_2048.max_active_requests}"` requests with `{python} f"{_cb_8k_2048.paged_internal_fragmentation * 100:.0f}%"` unused
- **Decode throughput:** paged at $p = 16$ runs about `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.speedup_vs_static:.2f}"`× static

Allocation policy matters only when memory binds. If the scheduler caps the batch below `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.static_max_active_requests}"`, both allocators admit the same requests and the speedup is 1.

Source: `ContinuousBatchingModel`. The Monte Carlo allocators in the [KV-cache tutorial](tutorials/03_kv_cache.qmd) admit the same `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.static_max_active_requests}"` and `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.max_active_requests}"` requests; the tutorial's throughput ratio is lower because its single random draw happens to give the first `{python} f"{_cb_8k_16.static_max_active_requests}"` requests a below-average length.
:::

Kwon et al. profile contiguous pre-allocation and find that only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV-cache memory holds token states. The rest is reserved slots for future tokens, internal fragmentation from over-provisioning for the maximum length, and external fragmentation from the allocator. PagedAttention limits each request's waste to one block [@kwon2023]. The static baseline here is max-length reservation, which captures the first two kinds of waste and is modeled without external fragmentation. Exact-size and power-of-two contiguous allocators, which trade reservation waste for external fragmentation, are not modeled. Sizing both allocators with every request at its full length is a peak-occupancy view: a request mid-generation holds fewer paged blocks, so paged capacity is conservative.

### 4.6 Serving Capacity Planning {#sec-serving-capacity}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.ServingCapacityModel`](api/solvers.ServingCapacityModel.qmd).*

Capacity planning composes three first-order quantities:

1. base request latency from `ServingModel`;
2. per-replica token throughput from `ContinuousBatchingModel`;
3. queueing delay from `TailLatencyModel`.

For an average response length $G$ tokens and per-replica decode throughput $R_{\text{tok}}$, the first-order request capacity is:

$$
Q_{\text{replica}} = \frac{R_{\text{tok}}}{G}
$$

The required replica count is the smallest $c$ such that traffic intensity remains stable and:

$$
P99_{\text{request}} \approx T_{\text{base}} + P99_{\text{queue}}(Q, Q_{\text{replica}}, c)
\le T_{\text{target}}
$$

Per-replica throughput $R_{\text{tok}}$ comes from paged allocation in [KV Allocation and Batch Capacity](#sec-batching), so passing `mean_request_tokens` below `max_seq_len` raises the batch each replica can hold. Base latency is then evaluated at the mean request length. This is deliberately a capacity model. It does not simulate request arrivals, preemption, or scheduler internals.

### 4.7 Serving Cost Dominance

At production scale, serving costs dominate training:

$$
C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{training}} + C_{\text{serving}} \times T_{\text{deploy}} \times Q_{\text{rate}}
$$

A 70B model costing \$2M to train, serving 1M daily users at 50 requests/day, costs ~\$18M/year in inference, 9× the training cost in year one. This is why inference optimization (batching, quantization, speculative decoding) has outsized economic impact.

## 5. Datacenter Sustainability {#sec-sustainability}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.SustainabilityModel`](api/solvers.SustainabilityModel.qmd).*
**Slide Deck:** [Sustainable AI (Vol II, Ch 15)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_15_sustainable_ai.pdf){target="_blank"}

### 5.1 Total Energy

$$
E = \text{IT\_Power} \times \text{Hours} \times \text{PUE}
$$

**Power Usage Effectiveness** (PUE) accounts for cooling and facility overhead. A PUE of 1.0 is theoretical perfect efficiency; hyperscale datacenters achieve 1.05–1.10 (liquid-cooled) to 1.4–1.6 (air-cooled). The industry average is `{python} f"{Infrastructure.Datacenters.Poland_Coal.pue:.2f}"`, meaning 37% of energy goes to cooling and power distribution, not computation.

### 5.2 Carbon Footprint

$$
C = E \times \text{Carbon\_Intensity}
$$

Where $C$ is in kg CO₂e and Carbon\_Intensity is in g CO₂e/kWh, sourced from regional grid data.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: Training Carbon Footprint

64 GPUs × `{python} f"{_a100_tdp:.0f}"`W × 336 hours = `{python} f"{_it_kwh:,.0f}"` kWh. With PUE 1.2 = `{python} f"{_tot_kwh:,.0f}"` kWh.

| Grid Region | Carbon Intensity | CO₂ Emissions |
|:------------|:----------------|:--------------|
| Quebec (hydro) | `{python} f"{_ci_quebec:.0f}"` g/kWh | **`{python} f"{_co2_quebec:,.0f}"` kg** |
| US Average | `{python} f"{_ci_us:.0f}"` g/kWh | **`{python} f"{_co2_us:,.0f}"` kg** |
| Poland (coal) | `{python} f"{_ci_poland:.0f}"` g/kWh | **`{python} f"{_co2_poland:,.0f}"` kg** |

Geographic choice alone creates a **~`{python} f"{_ci_spread:.0f}"`× difference** for identical workloads. Combined with hardware choice (5×) and quantization (4×), the total optimization lever is up to **800×**.

Source: Sustainable AI slides (Vol II, Ch 15).
:::

---

## 6. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) {#sec-tco}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.EconomicsModel`](api/solvers.EconomicsModel.qmd).*
**Slide Deck:** [Compute Infrastructure (Vol II, Ch 2)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_02_compute_infrastructure.pdf){target="_blank"}

$$
\text{TCO} = \underbrace{\frac{\text{Hardware\_Cost}}{\text{Depreciation\_Years}}}_{\text{CapEx (amortized)}} + \underbrace{E \times \text{Electricity\_Rate}}_{\text{OpEx (power)}} + \text{OpEx}_{\text{maintenance}}
$$

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: On-Prem vs. Cloud

| Metric | On-Prem (H100 Node) | Cloud On-Demand |
|:-------|:--------------------|:----------------|
| Unit cost | \$`{python} f"{_dgx_cost_k:.0f}"`K (amortize over `{python} f"{_amort_yr}"` yr) | N/A |
| Annual cost (80% util) | ~\$122K/node/yr | ~\$224K/node/yr |
| Effective GPU-hour rate | ~\$2.40 | ~\$`{python} f"{_cloud_gpu_hr:.2f}"` |

**Break-even occupancy:** ~55%. Below 55% sustained occupancy, cloud is cheaper. At 20% occupancy, on-prem costs ~\$6/GPU-hour, which is more expensive than cloud on-demand.

The right metric is **cost per useful TFLOP-hour**, not cost per GPU-hour. An H100 delivers `{python} f"{_h100_a100_flops_ratio:.1f}"`× the FP16 TFLOP/s of an A100 (or 6.3× comparing H100 FP8 to A100 FP16), so a higher sticker price may yield a lower effective cost.

Source: Compute Infrastructure slides (Vol II, Ch 2).
:::

## 7. Cluster Reliability (The Young-Daly Model) {#sec-reliability}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.solvers.ReliabilityModel`](api/solvers.ReliabilityModel.qmd).*
**Slide Deck:** [Fault Tolerance (Vol II, Ch 7)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_07_fault_tolerance.pdf){target="_blank"}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Intuition:** When training on thousands of GPUs for months, hardware failures are a statistical certainty. If a node fails, the job loses all progress since the last checkpoint. Checkpointing too often wastes time writing; checkpointing too rarely wastes time recomputing. The Young-Daly model finds the optimal balance.
:::

### 7.1 Cluster MTBF

Individual component reliability degrades linearly with scale:

$$
\text{MTBF}_{\text{cluster}} = \frac{\text{MTBF}_{\text{component}}}{N}
$$

| Cluster Size ($N$) | System MTBF (`{python} f"{_gpu_mttf_hr:,.0f}"` hr/GPU) |
|:------------|:----------------|
| 8 GPUs | ~8 months |
| 1,000 GPUs | `{python} f"{_mtbf_1k_hr:.0f}"` hours |
| 10,000 GPUs | **`{python} f"{_mtbf_10k_hr:.0f}"` hours** |
| 16,000 GPUs | **~`{python} f"{_mtbf_16k_hr:.0f}"` hours** (Llama-3 scale: `{python} f"{_llama3_failures}"` failures in `{python} f"{_llama3_days}"` days) |

### 7.2 Optimal Checkpoint Interval

$$
\tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \times \delta \times M}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------|:--------|
| $\delta$ | Time to write one checkpoint |
| $M$ | Mean Time Between Failures (cluster MTBF) |

### 7.3 Wasted Compute Fraction

The total overhead from checkpointing has two components:

$$
\text{Waste} = \underbrace{\frac{\delta}{2\tau}}_{\text{checkpoint writes}} + \underbrace{\frac{\tau}{2M}}_{\text{lost work on failure}}
$$

At the optimal $\tau_{\text{opt}}$, both terms are equal, and waste is minimized.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Worked Example: Llama-3 Scale Checkpointing

`{python} f"{_llama3_16k_gpus:,}"` GPUs, $\delta = 2$ min, cluster MTBF $M = 180$ min:

$$\tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \times 2 \times 180} = \sqrt{720} \approx `{python} f"{_tau_opt_min:.0f}"`\text{ min}$$

| Checkpoint Interval | Overhead |
|:-------------------|:---------|
| 10 min (too frequent) | 17% |
| **`{python} f"{_tau_opt_min:.0f}"` min (optimal)** | **7%** |
| 60 min (too rare) | 15% |

On a cluster costing \$10M/month, 7% overhead = \$700K/month. Async checkpointing (overlapping writes with computation) can reduce this to ~3%.

Source: Fault Tolerance slides (Vol II, Ch 7).
:::

---

## 8. Failure Probability {#sec-failure-prob}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.physics.calc_failure_probability`]({{< var github_repo >}}/blob/dev/mlsysim/mlsysim/physics/).*

The probability of at least one failure during a job of duration $T$ follows an exponential model:

$$
P(\geq 1\text{ failure}) = 1 - e^{-T / \text{MTBF}}
$$

For a 30-day training run on a cluster with MTBF of `{python} f"{_mtbf_10k_hr:.0f}"` hours: $P = 1 - e^{-720/`{python} f"{_mtbf_10k_hr:.0f}"`} \approx `{python} f"{_prob_30d:.1f}"`$, so failure is virtually certain. This is why checkpointing ([Section 7](#sec-reliability)) is not optional at scale.

---

## 9. Effective FLOPS (Fleet Goodput) {#sec-goodput}

*Implemented in [`mlsysim.physics.calc_effective_flops`]({{< var github_repo >}}/blob/dev/mlsysim/mlsysim/physics/).*
**Slide Deck:** [Performance Engineering (Vol II, Ch 9)]({{< var slides_latest >}}/vol2_09_performance_engineering.pdf){target="_blank"}

The actual useful computation delivered by a fleet after all overheads:

$$
\text{Effective\_FLOP/s} = \text{Peak\_FLOP/s} \times \underbrace{\text{MFU}}_{\text{per-GPU}} \times \underbrace{\eta_{\text{scale}}}_{\text{comm overhead}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{Goodput}}{\text{Rawput}}}_{\text{failure waste}}
$$

Each factor in the cascade represents a distinct loss mechanism. Typical values for large-scale training: MFU ≈ 0.3–0.5, $\eta_{\text{scale}}$ ≈ 0.4–0.85, Goodput/Rawput ≈ 0.85–0.97. The compound effect means a fleet may deliver only 10–35% of its theoretical peak.

---

::: {.callout-note}
## Limitations of First-Order Models

These equations are first-order analytical models. They assume:
(1) uniform memory access patterns, (2) no cache hierarchy effects, (3) no network contention under heavy load, and (4) linear scaling of throughput with batch size.

Real systems deviate from these assumptions. Trust MLSys·im for bottleneck classification and relative comparisons. Absolute latency is workload-dependent; well-calibrated cases are often within ±15–30%, while production serving can be 1.5–2× slower than idealized roofline bounds. See [Accuracy & Validation](accuracy.qmd) for detailed comparisons against MLPerf benchmarks.
:::
